# Comex Stat: the `join` that makes São Paulo disappear {#sec-m3-comexstat} ::: {.modulo-meta} **Data:** Comex Stat (MDIC), municipal export dataset and lookup tables **Downloaded by:** `R/preparar_modulo3.R` (@sec-m3), in the module's data package **Prerequisites:** @sec-m1-joins and @sec-m3-duckdb ::: Comex Stat is the most used public dataset for analysing Brazilian foreign trade, and it is where the most mistakes are made. This chapter walks through one specific mistake: a `join` that runs without complaining, matches 90% of the rows, and erases the country's largest exporting state from the report. ## The two datasets, and what cannot be combined The portal publishes two files per year and per flow, and they do **not** have the same granularity: | | `ncm/EXP_2024.csv` | `mun/EXP_2024_MUN.csv` | |:--|:--|:--| | Product | NCM, 8 digits | **HS4**, 4 digits | | Territory | state (`SG_UF_NCM`) | **municipality** (`CO_MUN`) | | Transport mode | `CO_VIA` | **not available** | | Customs unit of shipment | `CO_URF` | **not available** | | Statistical quantity | `QT_ESTAT` | **not available** | ::: {.callout-important} ## Municipality and transport mode do not exist in the same table This is not a limitation of the file you downloaded: it is the structure of the dataset. Any analysis of "municipal origin of cargo by mode" can only be done **by state**, assuming that the state's modal split holds for all of its municipalities. That assumption must be written in the report, not implicit in the code. Knowing what the dataset does **not** answer is part of the job, and finding it out before promising the product is the difference between a calm meeting and a bad one. ::: ## Step 1: Download ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dir.create("dados/brutos/comexstat", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) baixa <- function(url, arquivo) { caminho <- file.path("dados/brutos/comexstat", arquivo) if (!file.exists(caminho)) { utils::download.file(url, caminho, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) # the server returns a PHP page when the path does not exist, # and download.file() does not complain if (startsWith(readLines(caminho, n = 1, warn = FALSE), "<")) { file.remove(caminho); stop("Veio HTML/PHP em vez de CSV: ", url) } } caminho } arq_exp <- baixa( "https://balanca.economia.gov.br/balanca/bd/comexstat-bd/mun/EXP_2024_MUN.csv", "EXP_2024_MUN.csv") arq_mun <- baixa( "https://balanca.economia.gov.br/balanca/bd/tabelas/UF_MUN.csv", "tab_UF_MUN.csv") round(file.size(c(arq_exp, arq_mun)) / 1024^2, 1) #> [1] 54.4 0.2 ``` ::: Note that the lookup tables are **not** under `comexstat-bd/`, but directly in `bd/tabelas/`. It is a detail that costs half an hour to anyone who does not know it. ::: {.callout-warning} ## When MDIC's server fails In October 2026, the security certificate of `balanca.economia.gov.br` had expired, and `download.file()` failed with an SSL error (on Windows, `SEC_E_CERT_EXPIRED`). That is why the two files of this chapter come in the module's data package, copied from the server without changes. With them in `dados/brutos/comexstat/`, the function above downloads nothing: it just returns the path. Outside the course, if you need another year and the server is still like this, you can download without verifying the certificate. Only do this with public data, never with logins or confidential data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} curl::curl_download( "https://balanca.economia.gov.br/balanca/bd/comexstat-bd/mun/EXP_2023_MUN.csv", "dados/brutos/comexstat/EXP_2023_MUN.csv", handle = curl::new_handle(ssl_verifypeer = 0L, ssl_verifyhost = 0L) ) ``` ::: ::: ## Step 2: Read while keeping the leading zeros First the wrong way, the one anyone would use, letting R guess the types: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ingenuo <- readr::read_delim(arq_exp, delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE, locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1")) ingenuo |> dplyr::select(CO_ANO, CO_MES, SH4, CO_PAIS, SG_UF_MUN, CO_MUN) |> head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: `CO_MES`, `SH4` and `CO_MUN` became numbers. It looks harmless. It is not: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( cafe_original = "0901", cafe_lido = as.character(unique(ingenuo$SH4[ingenuo$SH4 == 901])[1]) ) #> cafe_original cafe_lido #> "0901" NA ``` ::: The HS4 code for coffee is `0901`. Read as a number, it becomes `901`. The same happens with **all** chapters 01 to 09 of the Harmonized System, which is exactly where Brazilian agribusiness lives: meat and coffee; soybeans, in chapter 12, escape, but sugar, fruit, cereals and fish do not. A `join` with the HS4 table loses all of this silently. The correct reading declares the types. The rule for this dataset is simple: **a field starting with `CO_`, `SG_` or `SH` is a code, not a number.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} con <- duckdb::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb()) exp_mun <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(" SELECT CO_ANO, CO_MES, SH4, CO_PAIS, SG_UF_MUN, CO_MUN, CAST(KG_LIQUIDO AS DOUBLE) AS kg, CAST(VL_FOB AS DOUBLE) AS fob_usd FROM read_csv('%s', delim=';', header=true, all_varchar=true, encoding='latin-1') ", normalizePath(arq_exp, winslash = "/"))) mun_tab <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(" SELECT * FROM read_csv('%s', delim=';', header=true, all_varchar=true, encoding='latin-1') ", normalizePath(arq_mun, winslash = "/"))) duckdb::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE) dim(exp_mun) #> [1] 1144828 8 ``` ::: `all_varchar=true` reads everything as text, and only what really is a number is converted afterwards. It is more work and it is the only safe way. ## Step 3: The anchor totals Before any `join`, record what you will check against: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ancora <- exp_mun |> dplyr::summarise( linhas = dplyr::n(), municipios = dplyr::n_distinct(CO_MUN), fob_bilhoes = sum(fob_usd) / 1e9 ) ancora |> knitr::kable(digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | linhas| municipios| fob_bilhoes| |-------:|----------:|-----------:| | 1144828| 2500| 337| ::: ::: ## Step 4: The `join` that "works" The municipality table has a column called `CO_MUN_GEO`. The name suggests an IBGE geocode, so the temptation is to join it directly with `geobr`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_br.gpkg" if (!file.exists(arquivo)) { br <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "all", year = 2022, simplified = TRUE, showProgress = FALSE) sf::st_write(br, arquivo, quiet = TRUE) } muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE) |> dplyr::mutate(code_muni = as.character(code_muni)) por_municipio <- exp_mun |> dplyr::summarise(fob_usd = sum(fob_usd), .by = CO_MUN) ingenuo_join <- por_municipio |> dplyr::left_join(sf::st_drop_geometry(muni), by = c("CO_MUN" = "code_muni")) c( linhas = nrow(ingenuo_join), casaram = sum(!is.na(ingenuo_join$name_muni)), pct_casaram = round(100 * mean(!is.na(ingenuo_join$name_muni)), 1), pct_fob_casado = round(100 * sum(ingenuo_join$fob_usd[!is.na(ingenuo_join$name_muni)]) / sum(ingenuo_join$fob_usd), 1) ) #> linhas casaram pct_casaram pct_fob_casado #> 2500.0 1913.0 76.5 71.9 ``` ::: No error. No warning. More than 85% of the municipalities matched. Whoever stops here publishes the map. ## Step 5: The investigation The habit from @sec-m1-joins: **always look at what was left out.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nao_casaram <- ingenuo_join |> dplyr::filter(is.na(name_muni)) |> dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(mun_tab, CO_MUN_GEO, NO_MUN, SG_UF), by = c("CO_MUN" = "CO_MUN_GEO")) nao_casaram |> dplyr::summarise(municipios = dplyr::n(), fob_bilhoes = sum(fob_usd) / 1e9, .by = SG_UF) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(fob_bilhoes)) |> knitr::kable(digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |SG_UF | municipios| fob_bilhoes| |:-----|----------:|-----------:| |SP | 445| 76.2| |GO | 84| 10.9| |MS | 55| 7.6| |DF | 1| 0.1| |ND | 1| 0.0| |EX | 1| 0.0| ::: ::: It is not scattered noise. It is **four whole states**, and one of them is São Paulo. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nao_casaram |> dplyr::slice_max(fob_usd, n = 5) |> dplyr::transmute(CO_MUN, NO_MUN, SG_UF, fob_bilhoes = round(fob_usd / 1e9, 2)) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |CO_MUN |NO_MUN |SG_UF | fob_bilhoes| |:-------|:---------------------|:-----|-----------:| |3448500 |SANTOS |SP | 6.68| |3450308 |SAO PAULO |SP | 5.21| |3448708 |SAO BERNARDO DO CAMPO |SP | 3.74| |3449904 |SAO JOSE DOS CAMPOS |SP | 3.68| |5318805 |RIO VERDE |GO | 3.21| ::: ::: Jundiaí appears in Comex as `3425904`. In IBGE, Jundiaí is `3525904`. The last five digits are the same; what changes is the **state prefix**. ## Step 6: The fix Comex Stat uses its own state numbering, which matches IBGE's in 23 states and differs in four: | State | Comex | IBGE | |:--|:--|:--| | São Paulo | 34 | 35 | | Mato Grosso do Sul | 52 | 50 | | Goiás | 53 | 52 | | Distrito Federal | 54 | 53 | There are also two codes with no territory: `93` (EX, an operation not assigned to a municipality) and `99` (ND, not declared). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prefixo_comex_para_ibge <- c("34" = "35", "52" = "50", "53" = "52", "54" = "53") co_mun_comex_para_ibge <- function(co_mun) { co_mun <- as.character(co_mun) prefixo <- substr(co_mun, 1, 2) sufixo <- substr(co_mun, 3, 7) novo <- prefixo_comex_para_ibge[prefixo] prefixo <- ifelse(is.na(novo), prefixo, novo) out <- paste0(prefixo, sufixo) out[substr(co_mun, 1, 2) %in% c("93", "99")] <- NA_character_ out } stopifnot( co_mun_comex_para_ibge("3106705") == "3106705", # Betim/MG, unchanged co_mun_comex_para_ibge("3425904") == "3525904" # Jundiaí/SP, changes ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrigido <- por_municipio |> dplyr::mutate(code_muni = co_mun_comex_para_ibge(CO_MUN)) |> dplyr::left_join(sf::st_drop_geometry(muni), by = "code_muni") c( pct_municipios = round(100 * mean(!is.na(corrigido$name_muni)), 1), pct_fob = round(100 * sum(corrigido$fob_usd[!is.na(corrigido$name_muni)]) / sum(corrigido$fob_usd), 1) ) #> pct_municipios pct_fob #> 99.9 100.0 ``` ::: ## Step 7: Checking A correct `join` cannot have created or lost rows, and the total must match the anchor from step 3: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( linhas_antes = nrow(por_municipio), linhas_depois = nrow(corrigido), fob_antes_bi = round(sum(por_municipio$fob_usd) / 1e9, 3), fob_depois_bi = round(sum(corrigido$fob_usd) / 1e9, 3) ) #> linhas_antes linhas_depois fob_antes_bi fob_depois_bi #> 2500.000 2500.000 337.046 337.046 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrigido |> dplyr::filter(is.na(name_muni)) |> dplyr::summarise(casos = dplyr::n(), fob_bilhoes = sum(fob_usd) / 1e9) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | casos| fob_bilhoes| |-----:|-----------:| | 2| 0| ::: ::: What is left without a match are the `EX` and `ND` codes, which **are not territory**. They must not go on the map, but they cannot vanish from the total either: the map's sum plus the non-territorial codes must reproduce the country's total exports. ## Step 8: The map, now defensible ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mapa <- muni |> dplyr::left_join( corrigido |> dplyr::select(code_muni, fob_usd) |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(code_muni)), by = "code_muni" ) |> dplyr::mutate(fob_bi = fob_usd / 1e9) ggplot2::ggplot(mapa) + ggplot2::geom_sf(ggplot2::aes(fill = fob_bi), colour = NA) + ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", na.value = "grey92", labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)) + ggplot2::labs(fill = "US$ billion (log)", title = "Exports by municipality, 2024", subtitle = "Domicile of the exporting company, not the place of production") + ggplot2::theme_void(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Brazilian exports in 2024 by municipality of the exporting company's domicile.](m3-02b-comexstat_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=1200} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## The municipality is the company's, not the production's This is Comex Stat's third trap, and it is conceptual, not technical. The municipality recorded is the **tax domicile of the exporting company**. A trading company headquartered in São Paulo that exports soybeans from Mato Grosso appears as São Paulo. For cargo-origin analysis, this rules out the municipal data as a proxy for production. The chart's subtitle above is not decoration: it is the caveat that stops someone from using the map for the wrong question. ::: ## Checklist ::: {.callout-tip} ## Before trusting any `join` with a federal dataset 1. **Declare the types when reading.** A code field is text. A leading zero is information. 2. **Count before and after.** The `join` cannot create or lose rows without you knowing. 3. **Always look at what was left out.** And look at it *grouped*: if the unmatched rows concentrate in one state, one year or one type, it is not noise, it is a system. 4. **Do not trust the column name.** `CO_MUN_GEO` is not the IBGE geocode. 5. **Check the total against the anchor.** The map's sum plus what is not territory must reproduce the country's total. ::: ## Exercise The `UF_MUN.csv` table has 5,570 rows, two of which are the special codes `EX` and `ND`. That leaves 5,568 municipalities, while IBGE recognises 5,570. Find out which municipalities are missing from the Comex table, by comparing with `geobr`, and explain what would happen to a historical series study that used this table as its reference register.
